issues.legal_issue: A village body may use vested village common land for any purpose authorized for that land, including leasing it for cultivation, without having to preserve land previously used for grazing for that use alone.
material_facts: The disputed land was village common land vested in the Gram Panchayat and was described as charand land used for grazing.
The appellants sought to prevent the Gram Panchayat from leasing the land and to have it kept for grazing.
The governing rules permitted use of the vested land for specified purposes, including grazing and leasing for cultivation.
issues.conclusion: The Gram Panchayat could use the land for any purpose specified in the rules, including leasing it for cultivation; prior use as grazing land did not require it to remain grazing land.
issues.legal_principle: Under Rule 3(2) of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Rules, 1964, a Gram Panchayat may use vested shamilat-deh land itself or through another for any of the listed purposes, including grazing and leasing for cultivation. The Court approved the interpretation in Khushi Puri v. State of Haryana, upheld by the Full Bench in Bishamber Dayal v. State of Haryana, and noted the consistent approach in Salig Ram v. Maksudan Singh.

predicates.village_common_land_use_dispute: The proceeding challenges a village body's use or management of village common land.
predicates.land_vested_in_village_body: The land at issue is vested in the village body.
predicates.intended_use_is_authorized: The village body's intended use is among the purposes authorized for the land.
predicates.village_body_may_use_land_for_authorized: The village body may use the land for the authorized purpose.

issues.definition: When a dispute concerns village common land vested in a village body and the intended use is authorized, the village body may use the land for that purpose.

issues.legal_issue: Land recorded as charand is included within village common land and is not a distinct category that cannot vest in the village body.
material_facts: The disputed land was described in the revenue records as charand.
The land was treated as shamilat-deh and had vested in the Gram Panchayat.
The appellants argued that charand land was distinct from shamilat-deh and could not vest in the Gram Panchayat.
issues.conclusion: Charand land is included in shamilat-deh, and the appellants' argument that the two categories were distinct was based on a wrong assumption.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(g) of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulations) Act, 1961 includes land described in the revenue record as shamilat-deh or, in Haryana, charand, subject to the stated exclusion for abadi deh. The Court relied on Khushi Puri v. State of Haryana, whose interpretation was upheld in Bishamber Dayal v. State of Haryana.

predicates.charand_land_status_dispute: The proceeding disputes whether land described as charand belongs to the category of village common land.
predicates.land_recorded_as_charand: The land is recorded as charand.
predicates.charand_is_included_in_village_common_la: Land recorded as charand is included in village common land.

issues.definition: When a dispute concerns the status of land recorded as charand, that land is included in village common land.

issues.legal_issue: A constitutional challenge to the vesting of village land is not established when the pleadings contain no supporting allegations for that challenge.
material_facts: The appellants argued that reserving charand land for the Gram Panchayat's income violated the constitutional protection they invoked and that compensation at market value was required.
The Court could not identify any averments in the writ petition alleging the asserted constitutional violation, despite asking counsel to point them out.
The appellants relied on Bhagat Ram v. State of Punjab.
issues.conclusion: The reliance on the constitutional decision was misplaced and without basis in the case, because the writ petition contained no supporting allegations of the asserted violation.
issues.legal_principle: The Court did not decide the constitutional claim on its substantive merits; it held that the reliance on Bhagat Ram v. State of Punjab was misplaced because the writ petition contained no averments supporting the alleged constitutional violation.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_vesting: The proceeding challenges the vesting of land on constitutional grounds.
predicates.supporting_constitutional_allegations_ab: The pleadings contain no factual allegations supporting the asserted constitutional violation.
predicates.constitutional_challenge_not_established: The constitutional challenge is not established on the record.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge to land vesting is raised without supporting allegations in the pleadings, the challenge is not established on the record.

issues.legal_issue: A representative challenge to long-standing village land management may be rejected as not bona fide and delayed when the challengers or their relatives accepted benefits from the arrangement and the delay is unexplained.
material_facts: The inhabitants raised no objection to the land's vesting in the Gram Panchayat for about 34 years.
Some of the land had been leased to village proprietors since 1976 without objection from inhabitants.
Family members of the appellants, including a brother of one appellant, had themselves taken the disputed land on lease.
The Court considered that the appellants pursued legal proceedings after failing to obtain a lease for themselves or their relatives, and that the delay in approaching the court was unexplained.
issues.conclusion: The Court considered the representative action not bona fide and found the unexplained delay to be an additional reason supporting dismissal of the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on the appellants' and their relatives' prior acceptance of leasehold benefits, the long period without objection, the apparent motive for bringing the proceedings, and the unexplained delay in approaching the court.

rule.if: representative_land_management_challenge and long_acceptance_without_objection and challengers_or_relatives_received_benefits and delay_unexplained

predicates.representative_land_management_challenge: The proceeding is brought representatively to challenge the management of village land.
predicates.long_acceptance_without_objection: The affected inhabitants accepted the land arrangement for a long period without objecting.
predicates.challengers_or_relatives_received_benefi: The challengers or their relatives received benefits under the arrangement they later challenged.
predicates.delay_unexplained: The challengers did not explain their delay in bringing the proceeding.
predicates.challenge_may_be_rejected_as_not_bona_fi: The challenge may be rejected as not bona fide and delayed.

issues.definition: A representative land-management challenge may be rejected as not bona fide and delayed when the inhabitants accepted the arrangement for a long period, the challengers or their relatives benefited from it, and the delay is unexplained.
